definitions.type: spatial derivative matrix field on ℝ^n × (0,∞)
definitions.definition: D_xu has columns ∂_{x_j}u for j=1,...,n, with ∂_{x_j} the componentwise partial derivative in coordinate j; ∂_{x_jx_j}u denotes its second derivative in that coordinate. Derivatives of u_t use the same convention. Its Frobenius square is |D_xu|²=Σ_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|².

e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|²+Σ_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u(x,t)|². Norms and dot products throughout are Euclidean; all spatial integrals are Lebesgue integrals, written dx. Write e_t for the time partial derivative of e.

inputs.statement: u:ℝ^n × (0,∞) → ℝ^m is jointly C^∞ (smooth) on this open domain.
For every pair of real times 0<s<t<∞ there exists a compact C⊂ℝ^n such that u(x,r)=q for every x∉C and every r∈[s,t].

output.statement: For every t0>0, let J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. There exist a compact C⊂ℝ^n and R>0 such that C⊂(−R,R)^n and u(x,r)=q for x∉C and r∈J. Put Q=[−R,R]^n; Q has finite Lebesgue measure (2R)^n. All positive-order derivatives of u vanish on (ℝ^n∖C)×int J. For every r∈int J, each of e(·,r), e_t(·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_tt(·,r), and, for j=1,...,n, ∂_{x_j}u(·,r)·∂_{x_j}u_t(·,r), u_t(·,r)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(·,r), and ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u)(·,r) is continuous, zero outside C, bounded on Q and absolutely Lebesgue integrable on ℝ^n. In particular e(·,t) is integrable for every t>0. The fields e and e_t are jointly continuous on ℝ^n×(0,∞).

argument.text: Fix t0>0 and set J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. Both endpoints are positive and the first is strictly smaller than the second. Apply H006 to these two times to obtain a compact set outside which u=q throughout J.

produces.statement: There exists a compact C⊂ℝ^n with u(x,r)=q for every x∉C and r∈J.

argument.text: Choose such a compact C from F001. Compact subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space are bounded: for example the increasing family of open boxes with positive integral radii covers C, and a finite subcover puts C in one such box. Enlarging its radius if needed gives a positive radius with strict containment in the open box. This also covers C empty.

Choose R as in F002 and set Q=[−R,R]^n. Its Lebesgue measure is (2R)^n<∞. The complement of compact C is open. On the open set (ℝ^n∖C)×int J the map u is the constant q by F001. H002 implies that all positive-order derivatives vanish on that open set. Thus at interior times e, e_t and the products u_t·u_tt, ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t, u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u and ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u), for every j vanish outside C. Products and finite sums of smooth derivatives are continuous; in particular e and e_t are jointly continuous on the original open space-time domain.

produces.statement: Q has finite measure (2R)^n and C⊂int Q. All positive-order derivatives of u vanish on (ℝ^n∖C)×int J. The fields e,e_t and the products u_t·u_tt, ∂_{x_j0}u·∂_{x_j0}u_t, u_t·∂_{x_j0x_j0}u and ∂_{x_j0}(u_t·∂_{x_j0}u), j0=1,...,n, are jointly continuous and zero outside C at interior times.

argument.text: At any r∈int J, each spatial function in question is continuous, hence Lebesgue measurable, and bounded on compact Q. Its absolute value is bounded by a finite nonnegative constant times the indicator of Q, since it vanishes outside C⊂Q. The integral of that bound is the constant times (2R)^n, which is finite. This proves absolute integrability of e(·,r), e_t(·,r), u_t·u_tt, ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t, u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u, and ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u), for every spatial index j. No interchange of a derivative and an integral is used here.

produces.statement: For every r0∈int J, e(·,r0), e_t(·,r0), u_t(·,r0)·u_tt(·,r0), and, for each j0∈{1,...,n}, ∂_{x_j0}u(·,r0)·∂_{x_j0}u_t(·,r0), u_t(·,r0)·∂_{x_j0x_j0}u(·,r0), and ∂_{x_j0}(u_t·∂_{x_j0}u)(·,r0) are continuous, bounded on Q, zero outside C and absolutely integrable on ℝ^n.

argument.text: Since t0∈int J, F004 in particular proves integrability of e(·,t0). Generalize the arbitrary t0 and existentially retain the compatible C,R and their box Q, together with F001–F004, to obtain the full quantified support and integrability assertion. Joint continuity of e and e_t was established in S003 using H002. The energy integral has therefore been proved finite at every positive time, before introducing the finite energy function.
